prompts.promptVerbatim: Anatomy and function of the GI system components; normal intestinal flora
prompts.supported: The digestive tract moves material from mouth to anus while accessory organs supply secretions. Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and outer covering provide distinct layers. Villi and microvilli enlarge the absorbing surface; the large intestine recovers water and electrolytes. Acid, bile, movement and antibodies help shape the microbial distribution. The liver processes absorbed nutrients; the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; the exocrine pancreas supplies enzymes and alkaline fluid.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Complete flora functions and named-organism inventory are not supplied. Autonomic salivary direction and Meissner plexus location need instructor clarification before testing.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know disorders of GI tract and accessory organs of digestion: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: Compare disorders by the disrupted function: an obstructed lumen prevents flow; an incompetent sphincter permits reflux; pancreatic enzyme loss impairs digestion; villous injury impairs absorption. Inflammatory bowel lesions differ in continuity and depth. Accessory-organ disease can change bile flow, hepatocyte processing or pancreatic enzyme delivery. The chapter cards below teach the supplied manifestations and broad treatments.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: The guide requests pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications for all GI/accessory disorders. Slides do not supply a complete disorder-by-component matrix or clinical protocols. See the detailed chapter topic ledger; absent prevention and diagnostic sequences remain gaps.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What protects the stomach?
prompts.supported: Mucus is a protective barrier at the gastric surface. Prostaglandins and nitric oxide protect this mucosal barrier. Protection must be distinguished from acid secretion: hydrochloric acid helps process food but is not the protective mucus layer.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Understand the process of digestion
prompts.supported: Digestion combines mechanical mixing with chemical breakdown. Salivary and pancreatic amylases process starch; pancreatic proteases act on proteins; emulsification separates fat droplets before lipolysis. Sugars and amino acids enter villus capillaries; absorbed lipid products leave through lacteals. Segmentation mixes contents against the surface, whereas peristalsis propels them.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Causes of pyloric stenosis
prompts.supported: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis narrows the outlet through enlarged pyloric muscle. The packet distinguishes increased cell size from increased cell number; both contribute in the notes to slide16. Family history, maternal gastrin and listed maternal factors are risk associations. Adult outlet obstruction can be acquired or congenital.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know dumping syndrome: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: After partial gastrectomy, a bariatric procedure or pyloroplasty, loss of reservoir and emptying control allows hypertonic chyme to enter the intestine rapidly. Early symptoms include cramps, diarrhea, fullness and nausea. Late symptoms at one to three hours include weakness, sweating and confusion. The supplied dietary strategy uses small frequent meals, more protein and fewer carbohydrates, and fluids between meals.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know different types of diarrhea-causes
prompts.supported: Osmotic diarrhea follows a nonabsorbed substance drawing water into the lumen. Secretory diarrhea reflects secretion of chloride/bicarbonate-rich fluid or reduced net sodium absorption. Excessive motility reduces transit time and the opportunity for absorption. Lactase deficiency illustrates the osmotic route: unabsorbed lactose contributes to diarrhea and gas.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Complications of diarrhea in children
prompts.supported: Children have lower fluid reserves than adults, so prolonged diarrhea can rapidly threaten hydration. The packet emphasizes replacing fluids and electrolytes and maintaining nutrition. General diarrhea consequences include electrolyte imbalance, metabolic acidosis and weight loss.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know intestinal obstruction: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: Distinguish a lesion blocking the bowel from functional failure of motility. Adhesions are a common small-bowel cause; large-bowel causes include cancer, volvulus and strictures. Obstruction level changes the pattern of distention and vomiting. In children, congenital narrowing, malrotation, Hirschsprung disease and intussusception provide different mechanisms. Telescoping bowel can compress its mesentery, obstruct venous return and progress to ischemic injury.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: A complete prevention/diagnostic algorithm and complication inventory by obstruction type are not provided.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know bilirubin: what is it? What is the bilirubin cycle?
prompts.supported: Bilirubin comes from breakdown of aged red blood cells. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble; hepatocytes conjugate it with glucuronic acid, making it water soluble (slide65 notes). Intestinal bacteria convert downstream bilirubin products to urobilinogen. Jaundice can reflect excessive production, hepatic processing disease or obstruction of bile flow.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know portal HTN in adults and children-what causes it and what happens because of it; what other structures are affected by Portal HTN
prompts.supported: Resistance to portal blood flow raises pressure. Collateral varices can appear in the esophagus, stomach, rectum and abdominal wall; rupture can bleed severely. Splenic enlargement can accompany thrombocytopenia. Ascites adds fluid to the peritoneal cavity. Pediatric extrahepatic disease commonly reflects portal-vein obstruction; intrahepatic disease is associated with cirrhosis or congenital hepatic fibrosis.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know GERD in adults and children: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: Adult GERD allows acid and pepsin to reflux through a weak or transiently relaxed lower esophageal sphincter. Increased abdominal pressure can contribute. Symptoms extend beyond heartburn to cough and laryngeal complaints. Infant reflux can reflect immature neuromuscular control and often resolves; persistent injury, bleeding, dysphagia or poor growth changes the concern.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Where are nutrients absorbed in the body?
prompts.supported: Villi and microvilli increase small-intestinal surface area. Major nutrient digestion and absorption occur in the small intestine. Sugars are primarily absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum. Water recovery occurs largely in the small intestine; products of carbohydrate/protein digestion enter capillaries, while lipid transport uses lacteals.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know cirrhosis in adults and children: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: Inflammation and fibrosis reorganize the liver and reduce function. Distortion and obstruction can raise portal pressure and shunt blood away from liver tissue. Alcohol-associated disease spans steatosis, hepatitis and fibrosis; biliary disease has different duct-related mechanisms. Pediatric cirrhosis can also impair growth, nutrition and development.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know cystic fibrosis (effects on the GI system)
prompts.supported: In cystic fibrosis, very thick mucus obstructs pancreatic ducts and limits digestive enzyme delivery. Pancreatic insufficiency produces maldigestion, especially of fat; growth failure can follow. The packet lists pancreatic enzyme replacement, high-calorie/high-protein intake and supplements. Pancreatic damage can involve beta cells and glucose regulation.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Celiac sprue: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, treatment (including diet)
prompts.supported: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy causes T-cell-mediated epithelial injury, inflammation and villous flattening. Reduced absorbing surface produces greasy bulky stools, poor growth and nutritional deficiencies. The packet lists serology and duodenal biopsy, then a permanent gluten-free diet and supplementation. Damaged villi can also produce temporary lactose intolerance.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know vomiting: trigger zones, different types, treatments
prompts.supported: The vomiting center is in the medulla. Retching is the action without expulsion; projectile vomiting need not be preceded by nausea or retching. Repeated vomiting can disturb fluid, electrolytes and acid-base balance. The obstruction-level examples distinguish clear gastric fluid, bile-stained fluid and later feculent material.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know all enzymes, hormones and secretions of the GI system-what cells secrete them, what do they do, what happens if there is not enough? Too much?
prompts.supported: Separate the source cell from its product and effect. Parietal cells provide acid, intrinsic factor and gastroferrin; chief cells provide pepsinogen; G cells gastrin; ECL cells histamine; D cells somatostatin. CCK links fat processing to slower emptying and gallbladder contraction. Pancreatic enzymes act on nutrient classes, whereas bile salts emulsify fat.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know anatomy of bone, know bone cycle
prompts.supported: Bone combines collagen-based tensile strength with mineral rigidity. Osteoblasts form osteoid, osteocytes coordinate maintenance and osteoclasts resorb bone. RANKL promotes osteoclast activity; OPG acts as a decoy. Remodeling alternates activation, resorption and new formation. Fracture repair proceeds through hematoma, procallus, callus, replacement and remodeling.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know bone growth in children
prompts.supported: Primary ossification centers develop in the diaphysis and secondary centers in the epiphyses. Growth continues at the physeal plate through endochondral ossification until closure unites epiphysis and metaphysis. Nutrition, general health, growth hormone and growth regulators influence the process.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know Duchenne muscular dystrophy: pathophysiology, etiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, and complications
prompts.supported: DMD affects dystrophin, which anchors the actin cytoskeleton to the basement membrane. Poor anchorage allows contraction-related membrane injury, calcium entry and fiber necrosis. Progressive weakness, Gower sign, respiratory insufficiency and cardiomyopathy are listed. Enlarged calves can reflect fat/connective tissue rather than effective muscle (slide61 notes).

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know all the different kinds of joints and fractures
prompts.supported: Classify a joint by movement separately from its connecting tissue. Synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis and diarthrosis describe immobile, slightly mobile and freely mobile joints; fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial describe structure. Classify a fracture by completeness, skin opening, orientation and mechanism. A torus injury buckles the cortex; a greenstick injury disrupts one cortex; comminution creates multiple fragments.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Individual named fibrous-joint definitions rely on a conflicted released key; its correction remains explicit. Full subtype geometry needs textbook figures where absent.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know parts of the joint: tendons, cartilage, synovium, bursa.
prompts.supported: Articular cartilage pads bony surfaces; synovial membrane lines the capsule; synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes. Tendons join muscle to bone and ligaments join bone to bone. Bursae are synovial-lined, fluid-filled sacs among tendons, muscles and bony prominences.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What part of a joint is insensitive to pain?
prompts.supported: Articular cartilage lacks vessels and nerves and is insensitive to pain. This does not mean that the whole joint is painless: its capsule is richly innervated.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know all parts of a muscle’s contraction.
prompts.supported: Excitation carries the action potential into the muscle; t-tubule signaling opens calcium-release channels. Coupling makes actin available to bind myosin. Cross-bridge action shortens the sarcomere; relaxation follows detachment and calcium return to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Complete troponin/tropomyosin and ATP-binding/hydrolysis sequence is not supplied.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Understand types of muscle contraction.
prompts.supported: In isometric contraction, tension increases while muscle length stays constant and the limb does not move. Dynamic contraction changes length: concentric shortens and eccentric lengthens. The agonist contracts as prime mover while the antagonist relaxes.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What controls muscle contraction?
prompts.supported: The CNS controls voluntary skeletal muscle through motor units. A unit consists of an anterior horn cell, its axon and supplied muscle fibers. Recruitment and discharge frequency grade force; spindles signal stretching. Calcium-release channels link the electrical signal to contractile availability.

prompts.promptVerbatim: What minerals are stored in bone?
prompts.supported: Calcium and phosphate form the inorganic mineral component of bone. Mineralization follows matrix production; hydroxyapatite is the named end product.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Understand muscle weight.
prompts.supported: The packet contrasts muscle as about 25% of infant body weight with 40% in adults. Muscle distribution changes with growth; fibers enlarge as fibrils become more numerous. Separately, the muscle tissue composition is about 75% water and 20% protein. Do not confuse tissue composition with percentage of body weight.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know Osgood-Schlatter disease: pathophysiology, etiology, prevention, clinical manifestations, diagnostics, treatment and complications
prompts.supported: Osgood-Schlatter disease involves the tibial tubercle and anterior patellar tendon. Activity-related pain, swelling and pressure tenderness guide the comparison. The supplied treatment reduces strenuous activity; persistent pain may require a cast or brace.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Specific prevention, diagnostic testing and long-term complications are not supplied. Broad osteochondrosis vascular wording needs instructor clarification before a precise causal claim is scored.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Know osteomyelitis: pathophysiology, etiology, clinical manifestations
prompts.supported: Osteomyelitis is bone infection that can spread beneath periosteum and into marrow. Loss of blood supply creates dead bone (sequestrum), while new periosteal bone is involucrum. Infants can stop moving a limb; older children can develop fever, swelling and reduced weightbearing.

prompts.promptVerbatim: Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis: pathophysiology, etiology, clinical manifestations
prompts.supported: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis shares inflammatory joint injury with adult RA but differs in presentation. The packet highlights larger joints, less severe pain, cervical changes and chronic uveitis; rheumatoid factor is seldom detected.
prompts.remainingGapOrLimit: Full etiology and subtype criteria are incomplete; slide34 leaves exactly five joints undefined. Blanket antibody/nodule statements need clarification and are excluded from scored keys.
